title: DNS Zone Transfer (AXFR) with Dig: TCP 53 EOF vs RFC-compliant refusal
summary: Tested DNS zone transfers (AXFR) using dig against xneelo's authoritative nameservers (ns1/ns2.host-h.net) and compared the behavior against enterprise infrastructure (Facebook). The tests revealed two distinct hardening mechanisms: xneelo forcefully drops TCP port 53 connections resulting in 'end of file' errors, whereas enterprise DNS completes the TCP handshake, returns the initial SOA record, and formally responds with a protocol-level refusal (Transfer failed). Neither server permitted zone disclosure.

blocks.label: kali
blocks.text:
$ dig axfr @ns1.host-h.net radblok.co.za
;; communications error to 129.232.248.30#53: end of file
;; communications error to 129.232.248.30#53: end of file
;; communications error to 129.232.248.30#53: end of file
;; no servers could be reached

$ dig axfr facebook.com @A.NS.FACEBOOK.COM
facebook.com.   3600    IN      SOA     a.ns.facebook.com. dns.facebook.com. ...
; Transfer failed.
Two completely different rejection signatures when attempting to transfer a zone. Understanding why they look different requires looking at how DNS works at Layer 4 (Transport).

sections.h: Why AXFR uses TCP port 53 instead of UDP

blocks.text: Almost all routine DNS lookups (`A`, `MX`, `TXT`) use **UDP port 53**. UDP is stateless, lightweight, and fast, but legacy UDP DNS packets are limited to 512 bytes (or ~1232–4096 bytes with modern EDNS0).

A complete DNS zone file containing hundreds or thousands of records can easily exceed hundreds of kilobytes. Therefore, RFC 1035 and RFC 5936 mandate that **DNS Zone Transfers (AXFR) must occur over TCP port 53** to ensure reliable, connection-oriented data transfer and retransmission.

head: Server Tested
Response from dig
Underlying Mechanism
rows: **Transport-level drop / TCP RST**. The firewall or BIND daemon at `129.232.248.30` accepts or intercepts the initial TCP connection on port 53, detects an unauthorized AXFR request, and immediately tears down the socket by sending a TCP FIN/RST packet without returning any DNS payload. `dig` receives 0 bytes from the closed stream, which it reports as `end of file`.

**Protocol-level refusal (RFC 5936)**. The nameserver completes the TCP handshake, echoes the start-of-authority (`SOA`) record to acknowledge the zone, and then explicitly transmits a DNS `REFUSED` (RCODE 5) header before terminating the transfer.

blocks.text: Both configurations are completely secure: neither server allows unauthorized zone transfers. The `end of file` signature is simply an abrupt network-level socket termination, while `Transfer failed` is an explicit, protocol-compliant rejection.

Resolving `radblok.com` returned `198.12.232.136`. This confirms `.com` is a completely different domain entity registered independently on a different network, whereas `radblok.co.za` is the target connected to Render/Cloudflare (`216.24.57.1`). Always double-check ccTLD vs gTLD boundaries during scoping.

items: Demonstrated how AXFR queries operate over TCP 53 to pull complete zone records.
Verified that both authoritative nameservers (`ns1/ns2.host-h.net`) strictly block zone transfers.
Identified the difference between TCP RST socket termination (`end of file`) and DNS protocol refusal (`Transfer failed`).
Confirmed that brute-force / dictionary enumeration is required since AXFR is blocked.
